current_text.html: When it is not convenient for a court to have the whole or perhaps any part of the testimony in any particular case taken in its presence, a commission shall be appointed, or coordinate court requested, to take the testimony in question, which shall be considered as if taken in the presence of the court. Due notice of the commission or coordinate court or videoconference, and of the time and place of its meeting, shall be given to the opposite party, that he may have an opportunity of attending. If the accused shall desire on his part to take testimony at a distance for his own exculpation, he shall give notice to the court of the time and place at which it shall be taken, in order that a commission or coordinate court, as in the former case, may be appointed for the purpose. Testimony may be taken on written interrogatories by filing the same with the clerk of the court having jurisdiction of the case, and giving two weeks' notice thereof to the adverse party, during which time he may file cross-interrogatories, if he desire it. Testimony shall then be taken by the commission or coordinate court in answer to the direct and cross-interrogatories, if such are filed, and no notice need be given of the time and place of taking the testimony.

occurrences.excerpt: …could be considered as a "refusal to testify" and thus violations of this BCO §35-12. We disagree. Rev. Nickoley remained in the presbytery until he was asked to leave. The undisputed fact is as stated in the ROC:

metadata.synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

Bruce Nickoley complained against Rocky Mountain Presbytery over its action dissolving the relationship with Evergreen Church. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order under SJC Manual 10.1. The same matter was already the subject of an appeal granted to Evergreen Church and docketed for Presbytery's January 22–24, 1997 meeting, and BCO 43-1 provides that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case in which an appeal is taken. No merits ruling was reached.

metadata.synopsis: TE Steve Newton appealed his conviction for contumacy and indefinite suspension from office by Heartland Presbytery's judicial commission for persistent failure to submit statistical reports and refusal to cooperate with Presbytery committees. The SJC affirmed Heartland Presbytery's judgment in all respects, with a concurring opinion finding three of four specifications invalid but deferring to the lower court's factfinding on the remaining specification.
